1651-1776

Caption This

Colonial Society and the Road to Independence

2

How this works (15–20 minutes)

  1. Look at each of the 5 images. Read the “What you’re looking at” line.
  2. Write a short, funny caption, like a meme. Pick a caption style if you want one.
  3. Then write 2–3 sentences about what is really going on. Use at least one key term from the lesson. Type the key term in English, exactly as shown.
  4. Save Progress any time. When all 5 are done, press Finished and upload the file to Canvas.

Keep it respectful: make the joke about the company, the idea, or the situation. Never joke about workers, children, immigrants, enslaved or freed people, Native peoples, anyone’s race or religion, or people who were hurt.

Image 1 of 5

A newly cleared farm

Not done

What you’re looking at: A hand-colored plan from Norton Ch. 3. A big field has been cleared of trees, and dark stumps are left all over the ground. Wooden fences cross the field. Small buildings sit at the top, in front of a forest. At the bottom, a man in a hat and a dog ride in a long, narrow boat on a river. Another person pushes the boat with a pole. Small numbers mark parts of the plan.

Heads up: This land was already home to Native peoples. Aim your joke at the stumps, the fences, or the hard work of clearing land. Never joke about the people in the boat, about Native peoples, or about anyone who worked this land.

  • Look at the stumps. What does this tell you about what the farmer did first?
  • Norton says land was cheap and workers were scarce. Why would a farmer want a big family?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Image 2 of 5

Profitable Fisheries

Not done

What you’re looking at: A colored print from Norton Ch. 3 called “Profitable Fisheries.” People work along a cold shore and on wooden platforms. They carry, clean, and lay out fish to dry on racks. A boat sits next to a tall wooden rack. At the left, a man in a thick coat holds a fishing line. A big sailing ship waits far back. Letters mark parts of the scene.

Heads up: Fish from this trade were also sent to the West Indies to feed enslaved laborers. Aim your joke at the fish, the drying racks, or the cold, smelly shore. Never joke about the workers or about enslaved people.

  • Look at all the racks and boats. What does this picture tell you about how New Englanders made a living?
  • Many New England farms had a short growing season. Why might people turn to the sea?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Image 3 of 5

A preacher and a crowd

Not done

What you’re looking at: A painting from Norton Ch. 3. A preacher in a black robe and a white wig stands high on a stone with both arms raised. A crowd of men, women, and children gathers around him. An older man in a blue-green coat bows his head. A girl kneels at the front. A woman at the lower left reads a book. A dog sleeps on the ground.

Heads up: Religion matters deeply to many people. Aim your joke at the dramatic pose, the crowd, or the sleeping dog. Never joke about anyone’s religion or beliefs.

  • Look at the preacher’s arms and the faces in the crowd. What mood does the artist show?
  • Look at the dog and the people in the crowd. What kinds of people came to hear him?

Image 4 of 5

Join, or Die (cartoon)

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white print from Norton Ch. 4. A snake is cut into pieces. Each piece has a letter label, like N.E., N.Y., N.J., and V. Under the snake are the words “JOIN, or DIE.” Norton says this cartoon is by Benjamin Franklin and first appeared in 1754.

  • Each piece of the snake has a colony’s letters. What do you think the snake stands for?
  • Read the words under the snake. What is Franklin telling the colonies to do?

Image 5 of 5

The Liberty Tree

Not done

What you’re looking at: A colored print from Norton Ch. 4. A huge tree stands on a hill. Two small dummies, called effigies, hang from its branches. A man points toward them, and a big crowd gathers below. Norton says angry colonists are hanging effigies of two tax collectors at a Sons of Liberty meeting.

Heads up: This is a serious one. The dummies hang from a tree. Write one clear line about the protest and the tax. No jokes about hanging, about violence, or about any person.

  • Look at the crowd and the tree. What kind of meeting does this seem to be?
  • The Stamp Act taxed paper. Who might be upset about that tax?
